summary: Andorra is a small landlocked country in the Pyrenees, sandwiched between France and Spain, whose heads of state are jointly the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell of Spain. It is known for ski tourism and tax-free shopping.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Since the Middle Ages Andorra has been jointly governed by the Catholic Bishop of Urgell and the French head of state (originally the Count of Foix); the 'Paréage' of 1278 established this system, and the bishop is still one of the two heads of state today. Catholicism is therefore inseparable from the state system, and although the 1993 constitution guarantees freedom of religion, it still specifically recognizes the status of the Catholic Church; about 80 percent of residents are Catholics.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: In the second half of the 20th century Andorra changed from a poor mountain region into a center of tourism and tax-free shopping; a large foreign population and the general secularization trend of Western Europe have reduced church attendance among the younger generation, and a little over one tenth of the population identifies as having no religion.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Other Christian denominations come mostly from foreign residents, such as Protestant churches of British and Nordic people, and groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses. Most of them are workers or retirees who moved in after the 1960s with the tourism, ski resort and financial industries.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Muslims are mainly migrant workers from North African countries such as Morocco, working mostly in construction and services. Because their numbers are very small, Andorra still has no formal mosque, and believers mostly meet in temporary places of worship.

religion.background: The Christianization of Andorra can be traced to the Visigothic and Carolingian periods, and legend has it that at the end of the 8th century Charlemagne granted the area autonomy in return for help against the Moors. In 1278 the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix signed the Paréage, and from then on the Catholic Church became part of state power. Until the promulgation of the 1993 constitution, Catholicism had a semi-official status. In recent decades, with the increase in tourism and immigration, religious diversity and secularization have gradually become evident, but church holidays and the feast day of the patron Virgin remain important national events.

language.official: Catalan is Andorra's only official language.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: More than half of Andorra's population is foreign, and Spaniards are the largest immigrant group, mostly arriving after the 1950s with the development of commerce and tourism. Because Spain is the main trading partner, Spanish is widely used on television, in shops and in daily communication, making it the most commonly spoken mother tongue.

ranking.name: Catalan
ranking.description: Catalan is Andorra's only official language; Andorrans themselves belong to the Catalan-speaking cultural sphere and have spoken it since the Middle Ages. The 1993 constitution established its status, and the government requires that public administration and commercial signage use Catalan, but because of the large foreign population, only three to four tenths of people have it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese speakers are mainly Portuguese laborers who immigrated in large numbers in the 1970s and 1980s, working in construction, hotels and ski resorts and gradually forming a sizable community. Their children mostly receive an education in Andorra, and the second generation can often use both Portuguese and Catalan.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French is spoken in the northern area bordering France, and Andorra's other co-prince is the President of France. There are French-system schools within Andorra, so some residents learn French at school, but only about 5 percent have French as a mother tongue.

language.history: Andorra lies in the Pyrenees, and in the Middle Ages it used Catalan along with the development of the Catalan region, while the co-principality system of 1278 also left it under long-term influence from both the French and Spanish sides. Before the mid-20th century Andorra's population was very small and almost all spoke Catalan. After the 1950s, the tourism and tax-free economy attracted large numbers of Spanish, Portuguese and French immigrants, and the linguistic composition quickly became diverse. The 1993 constitution established Catalan as the sole official language and, in education, runs three school systems side by side: Andorran, Spanish and French.

ranking.name: Trinxat
ranking.description: Cabbage and potatoes are boiled and mashed, then fried in a pan with bacon or pork belly into a flat round cake, crisp outside and soft inside; it is a plain, homely mountain dish.
ranking.history: Trinxat is a winter dish of farming households in the Pyrenees, and its name comes from the Catalan word 'trinxar' (to chop). Cabbage tolerates cold, while potatoes only became common in the mountains after the 18th century, and the two became important foods for the people of the barren highlands to get through the harsh winter. Today both Andorra and the neighboring Spanish region of Cerdanya regard it as a representative local dish.

ranking.name: Escudella
ranking.description: Meatballs, sausage, chicken and pork bones are stewed for a long time with chickpeas and vegetables; the broth is first eaten with pasta, and then the meat and vegetables are served separately.
ranking.history: This stew is one of the oldest dishes of Catalonia, and similar descriptions are already found in Catalan recipes of the 14th century. In Andorra and Catalonia it is traditionally the star of the Christmas lunch, called 'escudella de Nadal' (Christmas soup), in which large shell pasta (galets) are put. Its way of eating, soup first and meat afterward, also reflects the wisdom of old farming households in economizing on ingredients.

ranking.name: Botifarra
ranking.description: A raw Catalan sausage made mainly of pork, stuffed with salt and black pepper, usually charcoal-grilled or pan-fried and eaten with white beans or bread.
ranking.history: Botifarra is a traditional sausage of the Catalan region, connected with the custom in mountain households of slaughtering a pig in winter (matança del porc), when various sausages were made so they could be preserved through the winter. In Andorra, grilled sausage with white beans (botifarra amb mongetes) is a common home dish and is also a must at summer outdoor barbecues.

ranking.name: Crema Catalana
ranking.description: A custard cooked from milk, egg yolks, sugar, cinnamon and lemon peel; its surface is sprinkled with sugar and burned with a hot iron to form a crisp layer of caramel, and it is served chilled and sweet.
ranking.history: Crema catalana is often considered one of the oldest crème brûlée-type desserts in Europe, and similar desserts already appear in Catalan recipes of the 14th century. Traditionally it is eaten on 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph, and so it is also called 'crema de Sant Josep'. Andorra belongs to the Catalan cultural sphere, and this dessert is also a classic finish at local restaurants.

ranking.name: Pa amb Tomàquet
ranking.description: Ripe tomato halves are rubbed onto toasted bread, then olive oil is poured on and salt sprinkled; the method is simple but is representative of Catalan food.
ranking.history: Tomatoes are native to the Americas and only reached Spain in the 16th century; the method of pa amb tomàquet is generally thought to have appeared in Catalan villages in the 18th and 19th centuries, using tomato to soften hard bread that had been left for several days. It is one of the symbols of Catalan cultural identity and appears at almost every meal, served with ham, cheese or sausage. In Andorra it is likewise a basic accompaniment at breakfast and for snacks.
